note: Every source was opened and read on the checked date. Only verified sources may be linked from lessons (scripts/check-lessons.mjs enforces this).

sources.title: Halbjahresbericht 2025/2: Cyberbedrohungen in der Schweiz
sources.publisher: Swiss Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS)
sources.evidence: 29,006 voluntary reports in H2 2025; fraud 52%; SMS blasters used in Switzerland from summer 2025.

sources.title: Internet Crime Report 2025
sources.evidence: Victims aged 60+: 201,266 complaints, about $7.7 billion in losses. Elder fraud (60+): 201,266 complaints, $7.748 billion losses; Tech/Customer Support reported by 60+: 21,333 complaints and $1,040,730,043 losses (pp. 45–46). p.12: cryptocurrency investment fraud was the highest source of losses to Americans in 2025, $7.2 billion; contact via texts, social media, ads or dating apps, moved to a messaging platform; fake platforms show fake profits; when victims try to withdraw they are charged taxes and fees. pp.46–47 (60+): Investment 16,926 complaints, $3,519,296,354 losses; Confidence/Romance 10,188 complaints, $584,032,745 losses. p.40: over $19 million Confidence/Romance losses with a likely AI nexus; distress scams with voice cloning over $5 million.

sources.title: Protecting Older Consumers 2025–2026
sources.evidence: Reported losses by people 60+ over $3 billion in 2025. Older adults report losing far more to investment scams than any other fraud type; aggregate reported losses to investment scams jumped 42% in 2025, scammers often reach them on social media; because many frauds go unreported, reported amounts do not reflect the true cost.

sources.title: Schockanruf durch falsche Polizisten
sources.evidence: Crying voice, in some cases AI-generated; hang up, call the person directly or 117; police never ask for money by phone.

sources.title: Angebliche Polizisten rufen wieder ältere Personen an
sources.evidence: Manipulated numbers, even the police number; call 117 after hanging up and waiting for the dial tone.

sources.title: Vorsicht bei Telefonanrufen mit Bandansagen
sources.evidence: Press 1 connects to fake officer; Swiss mobile numbers spoofed; goal remote-control program; police never play recordings.

sources.title: Telefonbetrug
sources.evidence: “Legen Sie einfach auf!”; fake police steps; shock call; remote support scam; fake bank security.

sources.title: Phishing, Vishing und Smishing
sources.publisher: Swiss Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS)
sources.evidence: No bank asks by email to change passwords or verify card data; senders easily faked; report to antiphishing.ch.

sources.title: Finanzieller Schaden
sources.publisher: Swiss Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS)
sources.evidence: Contact bank immediately to block; many have 24-hour block hotlines; report to police. Re-checked 2026-10-26: if you notice or suspect financial damage act quickly and systematically: contact your bank or card provider immediately and have accounts or cards blocked; many providers have a 24-hour block hotline; report quickly to your bank and ask for the fraudulent payment to be stopped, have suspicious transactions checked and, where possible, reversed; the faster you act, the better the chances. BACS recommends a criminal complaint at the local police, ideally after phoning ahead; for payments abroad or in crypto the chances of recovery are usually much lower but a report is still important. TWINT payments are executed immediately and usually can't be reversed; adjust your TWINT limit in the app.

sources.title: Sicher twinten
sources.evidence: Staff never ask you to share passwords or access data; TWINT, its partners and your bank never ask for your security code; keep your PIN to yourself; enter it only in the TWINT app; scan TWINT QR codes only with the TWINT app, not the phone camera; don't pay with 5-digit codes someone sent you; payment links start with https://go.twint.ch/; send money only to people you know; check name, number and amount; be careful on marketplaces; if scammed call your bank immediately; forward suspicious mail to abuse@twint.ch.

sources.title: Report a cyber incident
sources.publisher: Swiss Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS)
sources.evidence: Not processed around the clock; acute emergency: call 112 or 117. Re-checked 2026-10-26: reports are not processed around the clock; in an acute emergency call 112 or 117. Voluntary notification: answer a few questions, get an automated initial assessment with measures, forward to the NCSC. Online criminal complaints only for listed offences (e.g. false flat ads, online purchase not received, data misused for orders); for all other offences contact a police station; the NCSC does not accept criminal complaints.

sources.title: 112: the European emergency number
sources.evidence: Free, works everywhere in the EU.

sources.title: Find help or report abuse
sources.publisher: US Department of Justice, Elder Justice Initiative
sources.evidence: If this is an emergency, call 9-1-1. Re-checked 2026-10-26: emergency call 9-1-1; for non-life-threatening emergencies: National Elder Fraud Hotline 1-833-FRAUD-11 (833-372-8311), 10 a.m.–6 p.m. Eastern Time, Monday–Friday; Eldercare Locator 1-800-677-1116.

sources.title: Scammers use fake emergencies to steal your money
sources.evidence: Voice cloning from a short clip; don’t trust the voice; hang up and call back on a known number. (WebFetch.) With a short audio clip, maybe from content posted online, and a voice-cloning program a scammer could sound just like your family member; they say it's urgent, you're the only one who can help, keep it secret; don't trust the voice; hang up or say you'll call back; ask a question only the real person would know; call on a number you know; call someone else in the family even if told to keep it secret; report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

sources.title: Criminals use generative AI to facilitate financial fraud (PSA)
sources.evidence: Create a secret word or phrase with your family. Generative AI increases believability; AI-generated audio: criminals generate short audio clips containing a loved one's voice to impersonate a relative in crisis asking for immediate financial help or ransom; AI-generated videos for real-time video chats with alleged company executives, law enforcement or authority figures, and to 'prove' an online contact is real; AI images for profile photos and fake IDs. Tips: create a secret word or phrase with your family to verify identity; look for imperfections (distorted hands or feet, unrealistic teeth or eyes, irregular faces, inaccurate shadows, lag time, voice matching, unrealistic movements); listen to tone and word choice; if possible limit online content of your image or voice, make social media accounts private, limit followers to people you know; verify by hanging up and calling the number directly; never send money to people met only online or by phone.

sources.title: How to recognize and avoid phishing scams
sources.evidence: Signs of phishing; contact the company on a number or website you know is real; forward to reportphishing@apwg.org.

sources.title: How to recognize and report spam text messages
sources.evidence: Fake package notices; companies won’t ask for account info by text; forward to 7726.

sources.title: Scammers hide harmful links in QR codes
sources.evidence: Don’t scan an unexpected QR code in an email or text.

sources.title: Caller ID spoofing
sources.evidence: Caller ID can be falsified; if a recording asks you to press a button, hang up.

sources.title: Cyber actors exploit “secure” websites in phishing campaigns (PSA)
sources.evidence: Do not trust a website just because it has a lock icon or https.

sources.title: Use strong passwords
sources.publisher: US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
sources.evidence: Long (16+), random, unique; passphrase of 4–7 words; use a password manager. Common identifying information, like birthdays and pet names, are not safe passwords.

sources.title: Turn on multifactor authentication
sources.publisher: US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
sources.evidence: Turn on MFA, starting with email.

sources.title: Have I Been Pwned
sources.evidence: Check if your email address is in a data breach.

sources.title: Make text easier to read on iPhone
sources.evidence: Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Larger Text.

sources.title: Report spam and block senders in Messages on iPhone
sources.evidence: Swipe left, Delete and Report Spam; Report Spam link for unknown senders.

sources.title: Screen and block calls on iPhone
sources.evidence: Settings > Apps > Phone: screen or silence unknown callers; block a contact.

sources.title: Use contacts from the Phone app on iPhone
sources.evidence: Add to Favorites.

sources.title: Add and use contact information on iPhone
sources.evidence: Contacts app, tap +, enter name and number, tap Done.

sources.title: Browse the web using Safari on iPhone
sources.evidence: Touch and hold a link to see a preview without opening the page.

sources.title: Bookmark a website in Safari on iPhone
sources.evidence: Add a bookmark.

sources.title: Use the Passwords app on your iPhone
sources.evidence: Passwords app from iOS 18; warns about weak, reused or leaked passwords.

sources.title: Use passwords on iPhone
sources.evidence: Security recommendations in the Passwords app.

sources.title: Find saved passwords and passkeys on your iPhone
sources.evidence: Open the Passwords app.

sources.title: Change text & display settings
sources.evidence: Settings > search Font size > slider.

sources.title: Report spam & block numbers in Google Messages
sources.evidence: Touch and hold the conversation > Block > Report spam > OK.

sources.title: See caller ID & spam protection
sources.evidence: More options > Settings > Caller ID and spam; Filter spam calls.

sources.title: Add, find & edit contacts on Android
sources.evidence: Contacts app > Add > name and number > Save.

sources.title: Manage passwords in Chrome (Android)
sources.evidence: Chrome offers to save; Google Password Manager; add a password.

sources.title: Manage passwords in Google Password Manager (Android)
sources.evidence: Save and manage passwords.

sources.title: Change compromised passwords in your Google Account (Password Checkup)
sources.evidence: Check if saved passwords are exposed, weak or reused; start Password Checkup.

sources.title: Make your account more secure
sources.evidence: Security Checkup; add a recovery phone and email.

sources.title: Create, find & edit bookmarks in Chrome (Android)
sources.evidence: More > Add to bookmarks.

sources.title: antiphishing.ch
sources.publisher: Swiss Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS)
sources.evidence: Report phishing pages via web form; forward phishing emails to reports@antiphishing.ch; run by BACS.

sources.title: Have I Been Pwned: Who, what and why
sources.evidence: Created and run by Troy Hunt since 2013 as a free resource.

sources.title: Turn on 2-Step Verification (Android)
sources.evidence: Open your Google Account > Security & sign-in > under 'How you sign in to Google' select Turn on 2-Step Verification > follow the on-screen steps; an extra layer of security in case your password is stolen.

sources.title: Two-factor authentication for Apple Account
sources.evidence: Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > turn on two-factor authentication; a six-digit verification code is displayed on trusted devices or sent to the trusted phone number; two-factor authentication is the default for most accounts.

sources.title: Passkeys
sources.evidence: FAQ: 'Passkeys are a password replacement technology … a passkey is a secret stored on one's devices, unlocked by the user the same way they unlock their device (biometrics, security key, PIN, pattern, etc.). Unlike passwords, passkeys are phishing-resistant, are always strong …'

sources.title: Sign in with a passkey instead of a password
sources.evidence: Sign in with fingerprint, face scan or screen lock PIN; passkeys can't be shared, copied, written down or accidentally given to someone else, so more secure against phishing; create: go to myaccount.google.com/signinoptions/passkeys > Create a passkey; only create passkeys on devices you personally own; anyone who can unlock your device can access the account; Android 9 / iOS 16 or later.

sources.title: Use passkeys to sign in to websites and apps on iPhone
sources.evidence: Passkeys are uniquely generated per account and less vulnerable to phishing; requires iCloud Keychain and two-factor authentication; when you see the option to save a passkey tap Continue; if no option the site doesn't support passkeys; sign in by tapping the account name field, the suggested name, then Face ID/Touch ID or device passcode; stored in the Passwords app.

sources.title: About the security of passkeys
sources.evidence: Passkeys are resistant to phishing, always strong, no shared secrets; public key stored on the server, private key never learned by the server.

sources.title: Sign in with backup codes (Android)
sources.evidence: Backup codes for when you lose your phone or can't get codes; each 8-digit code works once; a new set of 10 whenever you want, old set becomes inactive; do not share backup codes; Google never asks for a backup code other than at sign in; store somewhere safe like where you keep your passport; Settings > Google > Manage your Google Account > Security & sign-in > 2-Step Verification > Backup codes > Continue > Get backup codes.

sources.title: Set up a recovery contact for your Apple Account
sources.evidence: A recovery contact is someone you designate who can get a recovery code for you; they have no access to your account; Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Recovery Contacts > Add Recovery Contact; needs iOS 15 or later.

sources.title: S-U-P-E-R.ch – Carry out regular updates
sources.evidence: All software contains vulnerabilities; cybercriminals exploit them to take control of devices, infect them with malware and steal login or card data; activate the automatic update function for the operating system and all programmes and apps; use the latest browser version.

sources.title: Geräteschutz, Passwörter und Zugriffsschutz
sources.evidence: Make sure all devices install security updates automatically; outdated software is a gateway for criminals; only download software and apps from official manufacturer sites or official app stores; on mobile, download apps only from recognised stores and check ratings and permissions.

sources.title: Update Software
sources.evidence: Page marked as archived content. 'Many software updates are created to fix security risks'; turn on automatic updates in the device's or application's security settings.

sources.title: Update your iPhone or iPad
sources.evidence: Keeping software up to date is one of the most important things for security; Settings > General > Software Update > Automatic Updates > turn on Automatically Install (installs overnight while charging on Wi-Fi) / Automatically Download; back up, plug into power, use Wi-Fi.

sources.title: Check & update your Android version
sources.evidence: Connect to Wi-Fi, charge to at least 75%; most system updates and security patches install automatically; when notified, open the notification and tap the update action; or Settings > System > Software updates (Pixel); steps can vary by device.

sources.title: Install Windows Updates
sources.evidence: Windows 11/10: Start > Settings > Windows Update > Check for Windows updates > Download & install; restart if prompted.

sources.title: Update macOS on Mac
sources.evidence: Apple menu > System Settings > General > Software Update; Software Update automatically checks for new software; use Software Update settings to control whether your Mac downloads or installs updates automatically.

sources.title: Update apps or use automatic downloads on iPhone
sources.evidence: Apps downloaded from the App Store update automatically by default on iPhone and iPad; manual: App Store > My Account / your photo > App Updates.

sources.title: How to update apps on Android
sources.evidence: Updating apps improves app security; Google Play > profile picture > Settings > Network Preferences > Auto-update apps > choose an option.

sources.title: How to spot, avoid, and report tech support scams
sources.evidence: Fake pop-up warnings urge you to call a number; scammers ask for remote access, pretend to find a virus and charge a fee; they want gift cards, wire, crypto or payment apps; legitimate tech companies won't contact you to say there's a problem with your computer; real security pop-ups never ask you to call a phone number; talk to someone you trust; report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. (Fetched via WebFetch; direct fetch returns 404 to scripts.)

sources.title: Protect yourself from tech support scams
sources.evidence: Microsoft doesn't make unsolicited calls or send unsolicited email to provide tech support; Microsoft error and warning messages never include phone numbers; scammers may put the browser in full screen with pop-ups that won't go away; with remote access they install malware; download software only from official sites or the Microsoft Store.

sources.title: Falsche Sicherheitswarnung beim Surfen im Internet
sources.evidence: Fake security warning with a number; caller poses as Microsoft or Apple support, has victim install remote maintenance software, then leads to payment page or e-banking; do not call; Windows: Ctrl+Alt+Del, Task Manager, end the browser; Mac: Cmd+Option+Esc, Force Quit the browser; if you gave access: call bank, change passwords, have the computer reset, report to cantonal police.

sources.title: Woche 41: Entwicklung bei Fake Support
sources.evidence: Fake support: callers pose as IT firm such as Microsoft; browser lock pages with often Swiss phone numbers, sometimes a voice; neither browser nor computer is really locked; closing the browser or restarting helps; never call the number; never allow remote access; if you did, have a specialist check the computer.

sources.title: Woche 15: Falsche Bankmitarbeiter fordern Installation von Fernwartungssoftware
sources.evidence: 14 April 2026: rise in calls from fake bank staff (also BAKOM) who connect to an 'IT specialist' and push installation of AnyDesk, TeamViewer etc.; with access they see the screen, control the mouse, steal passwords and access e-banking; banks, card companies and authorities never ask by phone to install remote software; end such calls; uninstall and change passwords if installed; report to local police if money lost.

sources.title: Use Google Play Protect
sources.evidence: Play Protect runs a safety check on apps from Google Play before download, checks device for harmful apps from other sources, warns and may remove them; on by default; recommended to always keep on; Play Store > profile icon > Play Protect > Settings.

sources.title: App Store
sources.evidence: 'We conduct a thorough review to check that apps come from known sources, are free of known malware …'; App product pages show rankings and reviews.

sources.title: «Hallo Mama»-Mail lockt auf WhatsApp
sources.evidence: Fake 'son/daughter' says the phone is broken and they can only be reached on WhatsApp at a new number; pressure ('it is important'); after trust-building they urgently need money for a bill or transfer and give payment instructions (bank transfer, payment service, voucher/prepaid codes). Advice: don't use the 'new number'; call relatives on the number you know; ask control questions only they can answer, not ones findable online or on social media; don't transfer money because of a message.

sources.title: Übernommene WhatsApp-Konten: Betrüger versenden Links oder fordern Geld
sources.evidence: Criminals use taken-over WhatsApp accounts to message contacts; takeover not visible because messages appear in the existing chat with the same number and profile; they ask for money in chats or in the WhatsApp Status, and send links to fake sites to take over more accounts. Advice: check unusual requests through another channel; never pass on codes sent to you; don't follow links; use 2FA. If affected: Settings > Linked devices, log out unknown devices.

sources.title: Gefälschte Tanzabstimmung führt zu Zugriff auf das WhatsApp-Konto
sources.evidence: Message seemingly from someone you know asks for a vote for a young dancer; fake site asks you to 'verify' by scanning a QR code with WhatsApp, which links your WhatsApp account to the criminals' device. Advice: check unusual requests another way; tell contacts; Settings > Linked devices, log out unknown devices; if locked out, register again with your phone number.

sources.title: How to manage two-step verification settings
sources.evidence: (Fetched via WebFetch; scripts get HTTP 400.) WhatsApp is upgrading the 6-digit PIN to a password. Android: More (three dots) > Settings > Account > Two-step verification > toggle on Turn on two-step verification > create a strong password and confirm > add an email you can access (Next) or Skip > Trust this device or Skip. iPhone (cms_platform=iphone): You > Account > Two-step verification, same steps.

sources.title: About two-step verification
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) Optional feature that adds more security; by using two forms of authentication you protect against unauthorized access; you can choose phone number, password or email for additional authentication; passkeys also available.

sources.title: Received verification code without requesting it
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) WhatsApp notifies you when someone tries to register your number; can be a typo or an attempt to take over your account; 'you should never share your WhatsApp verification code with others'; without the SMS code, they can't use your number on WhatsApp.

sources.title: How to unlink a device
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) Android: More options (three dots) > Linked devices > tap a device > Log out. iPhone: Settings or profile picture > Linked devices > tap a device > Log out > Log out.

sources.title: Réseaux sociaux: ne divulguez pas trop d’informations personnelles
sources.evidence: Published 17 May 2026: scammers often collect personal information on social networks to personalise attacks; share personal information with restraint; don't post photos that could be used against you; data collectors build profiles from seemingly harmless details; the internet forgets nothing.

sources.title: Woche 32: Ferienerlebnisse teilen und bewahren
sources.evidence: AI makes it easy to manipulate pictures; the more images available, the easier deepfakes; think about what each post reveals; don't post photos of people without their consent; set the platform so only people on your friends list can see photos.

sources.title: Lassen Sie Einbrecher nicht von Ihren Ferien profitieren!
sources.evidence: 'Teilen Sie Ihre Abwesenheit nicht in sozialen Netzwerken' (don't share your absence on social networks); don't leave an absence message on the answering machine.

sources.title: That friend request could be from a scammer
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) 6 Oct 2023: since 2021 people reported losing $2.7 billion to scams that started on social media, more than any other contact method; scammers hack profiles, pretend to be you and con friends; use profile info like age and hobbies; use privacy settings to limit who sees your posts; don't reply to messages asking for money even if from a friend: call them to check.

sources.title: Can you spot an investment scam on social media?
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) 28 May 2025: a friend's account suddenly promoting quick-money investing is likely taken over; slow down, research, there are no guaranteed returns; tell your real friend by email or text.

sources.title: Report a Facebook profile or Page pretending to be you or someone else
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) Impersonating profiles aren't allowed; report: go to the profile > Options below the cover photo > Report profile > follow the prompts; possible without an account via a form.

sources.title: Social Media Hacking
sources.evidence: Attackers often use hacked accounts to target your contacts; change password; use the reset function; contact the provider; inform contacts through another channel; report identity misuse to police.

sources.title: Woche 7: Wie Prominente für Investment-Betrug missbraucht werden
sources.evidence: 18 Feb 2025: sites styled like news portals (often Blick, 20min, SRF, RTS) with made-up celebrity interviews promise wealth from small investments (usually CHF/EUR 250); spread via spam, social media (X, Facebook), YouTube ads; after registering a 'personal adviser' calls, fake growing balance, pressure for more; withdrawals need more 'fees'; later fake recovery offers. Advice: check you are on the real media site; check FINMA authorisation and warning list; never be pressured; stop contact; no more payments; report to cantonal police.

sources.title: Missbräuchliche Verwendung von Promibildern
sources.evidence: Spam and articles about celebrities (e.g. a fake report on Roger Federer) lead to trading platforms; after registering, a call centre 'broker' calls within minutes; fake early profits; withdrawals blocked; advice: check whether the firm has a FINMA licence; don't give anyone remote access.

sources.title: Warning list
sources.evidence: 'These companies are not authorised and may be engaging in financial market activity without the requisite licence.' Also links to the list of authorised institutions.

sources.title: Halbjahresbericht 2025/2 (PDF)
sources.evidence: p.6: more reports about fraudulent web shops that deliver no or inferior goods; many emphasise Swiss characteristics to build trust. p.11: phishing in the name of SwissPass and parcel services is still about 40 percent of all phishing URLs. p.16: classified-ads portals: criminals posed as buyers in a hurry, claimed to have paid, attached 'twint-rechnung.zip' infostealer malware. p.23: 824 reports of fraudulent web shops in H2 2025, 266 more than H1, peaks November–January (Christmas shopping); classified-ads fraud 462 reports.

sources.title: Woche 28: Betrügerische Websites erkennen
sources.evidence: Fake shops increasing; check reviews critically (many 5-star reviews can be a warning sign; bad reviews are most helpful; no reviews is suspicious); check the web address for typos and odd additions; search adverts can be fake; domains younger than three months reported to BACS are practically always fraud; check .ch registration date via nic.ch.

sources.title: Sicher online unterwegs
sources.evidence: Check unknown shops: read reviews; no reviews means a new shop, be careful; check the imprint for a plausible address, correct phone/email and valid commercial register number; prefer invoice to prepayment; avoid giving card numbers where possible, otherwise only on encrypted sites; check card statements and inform the card issuer of discrepancies; reviews can be fake; when selling, ship only after payment has arrived and don't trust payment confirmations by email; never enter e-banking login or card data on alleged shipping portals after a sale.

sources.title: Online shopping
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) Search the company name plus 'complaint' or 'scam'; pay by credit card when possible: it best protects you; https doesn't mean legitimate; you can dispute charges for items never received; never buy from sellers who insist on gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or crypto; keep records. Re-fetched 2026-10-26: 'don't rely on star ratings alone because some reviews and ratings are fake'; 'Paying by credit card best protects you'; https 'doesn't mean it's a legitimate site'; dispute a charge for merchandise never received: letter must reach the card company within 60 days of the first bill showing the error; 'If you have a problem when you shop online, try to work it out directly with the seller... If that doesn't work, tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.'

sources.title: 3-D Secure für sicheres Onlineshopping
sources.evidence: 3-D Secure (Mastercard Identity Check, Visa Secure): after paying online by credit card you receive an SMS code or a 3-D Secure notification in the Swisscard app to confirm the payment; after approval the payment is confirmed.

sources.title: Woche 40: Kleinanzeigen-Phishing – Angreifer verteilen neu Schadsoftware
sources.evidence: Fake buyer contacts seller, moves to WhatsApp (Swiss mobile number), sends a link or QR code to a fake PostFinance or payment-service page claiming the seller receives the money by 'confirming'; aim: card or e-banking data; new: 'Twint-Rechnung.zip' malware with pressure to open on a computer. Advice: treat files from buyers as malicious; never open attachments to confirm a payment; insist on your payment method; to receive money you never need to enter card details or confirm a code; check receipt in your own app or e-banking; don't trust screenshots, PDFs or emails; if infected disconnect, change passwords from another device, report to BACS and police.

sources.title: Recognize phishing: check real Swiss Post messages
sources.evidence: Official Swiss Post websites use post.ch, poste.ch, posta.ch, swisspost.ch or swisspost.com; Swiss Post won't ask for passwords, SMS codes or complete credit card details by e-mail, SMS or WhatsApp; no threats or extremely short deadlines; only download Swiss Post apps from the App Store or Google Play, never via a link.

sources.title: S-U-P-E-R.ch – Fake fees
sources.evidence: Fake parcel/customs messages say payment is awaited; the link leads to a phishing site for card details or a subscription trap; genuine delivery services and the customs authority do not collect postage or fees in this way; compare the consignment number and contact the delivery service or customs authority if in doubt.

sources.title: Angeblich nicht abgeholtes AliExpress-Paket führt zu Kreditkarten-Phishing
sources.evidence: Email claims an uncollected AliExpress parcel; phishing site asks delivery questions, then a CHF 1.95 shipping fee, personal details and card details; a fake error asks you to enter the card again or another card. Advice: don't follow links; if you gave data, call your bank and block the cards; report to police.

sources.title: European Consumer Centres Network (ECC-Net)
sources.evidence: Network of offices co-funded by the European Commission; if you live in the EU, Iceland or Norway, the ECC in your country can explain your rights, help settle a dispute with a seller in another EU country (or Iceland or Norway), and tell you whom to contact if they can't help. Switzerland is not listed.

sources.title: Wo finde ich Hilfe? (Wegweiser Online-Shopping)
sources.evidence: Ombudsstelle E-Commerce handles complaints about online purchases where no amicable solution was found, free of charge; consumers can usually sue at their place of residence; simplified, low-cost procedure starting with conciliation; SECO can act for collective interests under the UWG (complaint form) but cannot enforce individual refunds.

sources.title: Ombudsstelle E-Commerce
sources.evidence: Free help for complaints after an online purchase that you could not resolve with the company; requests via online form; phone 031 380 50 34 Mon–Fri 09:00–12:00; c/o Konsumentenforum kf, Belpstrasse 11, 3007 Bern.

sources.title: Einkaufen im Ausland (Wegweiser Online-Shopping)
sources.evidence: Foreign goods generally must be declared and are subject to VAT and customs; carriers like DHL, UPS or Swiss Post handle customs declaration and bill the recipient; a .ch domain does not mean a Swiss company — check the seller's identity (imprint); only .swiss domains are certainly Swiss companies or citizens; counterfeits can be seized at the border.

sources.title: Konsumenten-Helpline
sources.evidence: FAQ, list of ombudsman offices; written information form (not legal advice); helpline +41 (0)58 462 20 00, Monday, Wednesday and Friday 10:00–11:00.

sources.title: Think that text message is from USPS? It could be a scam
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) Texts claiming unpaid postage, a missed delivery or updated shipping preferences, from 'USPS (or FedEx…or DHL…)', link to look-alike sites; if you pay, the money and your card number go to the scammer; verify independently via the retail site or account you ordered from; forward to 7726; report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

sources.title: Smishing: Package Tracking Text Scams
sources.evidence: USPS will not send text messages or e-mails without the customer first requesting the service with a tracking number, and it will not contain a link; USPS does not charge for tracking; if you interacted with the URL notify your financial institution; report to spam@uspis.gov and forward to 7726.

sources.title: Romance Scam
sources.evidence: Fake profiles on social media and dating sites fake a love relationship; often claim they can't meet because they are abroad; after building trust they ask for money. Measures: end contact and block; if you lost money, BACS recommends a criminal complaint at the local police (find a station via Suisse ePolice); talk to a trusted person if it weighs on you; for money problems contact your canton's debt advice service. Prevention: send neither money nor goods to people you have never met.

sources.title: Woche 32: Die psychologischen Tricks der Betrüger – Teil 2
sources.evidence: 'handeln Sie nicht aus einem Schamgefühl heraus'; romance scams deliberately exploit loneliness and being in love; scammers pick people who suffer from loneliness; emotional bond makes later demands easier; many find it hard to get out alone; demands from someone you never met in person are a clear warning sign, especially money; refuse even if they threaten to break contact; 'Wer Sie wirklich liebt oder schätzt, wird Sie nicht emotional unter Druck setzen'; 'Emotionen sind menschlich – und genau das machen sich Betrüger zunutze.'

sources.title: Woche 14: «Romance Scam» im Wandel – Mit KI zur perfekten Täuschung
sources.evidence: Alongside online investment fraud, romance scams are among the phenomena with the highest losses; case: AI-generated images of the 'partner' in a hospital bed with a cup bearing the victim's name; worsening health updates, request for treatment money, then fake death notice and gravestone image, then promise of refund against fees. Recommendations: end contact once they repeatedly ask for money; police complaint; talk to a trusted person; debt advice; never send money or goods to people you never met.

sources.title: Woche 31: Die psychologischen Tricks der Betrüger – Teil 1
sources.evidence: Foot-in-the-door: whoever agreed to a small request is more likely to agree to bigger ones; people strive for consistency; just because you agreed to a small request doesn't mean you must keep agreeing; end contact. FOMO: investment platforms claim only a limited number of people can invest, creating fear of missing a unique chance.

sources.title: Romance Scam: Liebesbetrüger im Internet
sources.evidence: Modus operandi: quick declarations of love, relationship built over weeks and months via Skype, WhatsApp; just before a planned meeting an accident, illness or robbery, request to pay costs; new obstacles; if victim stops paying, pressure, sextortion, or a fake 'authority' or 'lawyer' offering return of money against an administrative fee. 'Machen Sie sich keine Vorwürfe ... die Polizei [ahndet] keine menschlichen Schwächen, sondern [fahndet] nach Kriminellen'; your report can protect other victims; bring all information. If victim: send no more money, report to police, end contact and block, don't react to supposed helpers (Interpol, foreign police, victims' lawyers), talk to a trusted person, seek psychological help, debt advice. If you know a victim: encourage police; if no insight and danger of financial hardship, cantonal adult protection authority (KESB).

sources.title: Romance Scam – Liebesbetrug über das Internet
sources.evidence: Perpetrators often pose as army generals, doctors or engineers abroad; daily charming messages, promises up to marriage; then ask for money for emergencies. Advice: don't accept friend requests from people you don't know in real life; be suspicious if they talk of great love before a first meeting; never transfer money to people you only know from the internet; check their photos with Google image search, reused images are a strong sign of fraud. Already paid: send no more money even under pressure; collect all documents (emails, chats); report to your cantonal police after phoning ahead.

sources.title: What To Know About Romance Scams
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) Scammers say they can't meet in person (abroad, oil rig, military); ask for money for medical expenses, tickets, visa; may offer to help you get started in crypto investing; tell you to pay by wire, gift cards, payment app or crypto. Bottom line: never send money or gifts to a sweetheart you haven't met in person. Stop communicating; talk to someone you trust; search the job plus 'scammer'; reverse image search the profile picture. If paid: contact the company or bank right away; report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to the dating site or app.

sources.title: Investment Scams
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) Crypto investment scams often start with a direct message on social media or dating apps; site or app isn't really investing; fake reports show money growing; urged to invest more; then accounts shut down. Signs: guaranteed profits or returns ('Only scammers will guarantee...'); little risk; few details; secret method; high pressure. All investments come with risk; no guaranteed returns. Before you invest, talk to someone you trust; check registration on Investor.gov. Report to ReportFraud.ftc.gov and SEC at sec.gov/tcr.

sources.title: What To Know About Cryptocurrency and Scams
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) Crypto stored in a digital wallet; if wallet lost or stolen, no one can step in to recover funds; not insured by government; values change constantly; payments typically not reversible, no legal protections like cards. Only scammers demand payment in crypto, not to buy something and not to protect your money; only scammers guarantee profits; never mix online dating and investment advice. Investment manager: fake website, can't withdraw or only with high fees. Government impersonators tell you to protect money by buying crypto, stay on phone and direct you to a crypto ATM and a QR code into their wallet. Report: ReportFraud.ftc.gov, CFTC, SEC, IC3, the exchange.

sources.title: Refund and Recovery Scams
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) Scams that target people who already lost money; scammers buy 'sucker lists'; claim to be government agency, consumer group, law firm; ask for upfront 'retainer fee', 'processing fee', 'tax'. Government agencies and legitimate organisations will never ask for money to help you get a refund and won't guarantee you'll get your money back. Never pay upfront; look up agency numbers yourself. Report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and state attorney general.

sources.title: What You Can Do to Avoid Investment Fraud
sources.evidence: 'Guaranteed returns' aren't: every investment carries some risk; high returns entail high risks, possibly total loss; fraudsters try to convince that returns are 'guaranteed' or 'can't miss'. Beware the 'halo' effect: credibility can be faked. 'Everyone is buying it.' Pressure to send money RIGHT NOW: resist.

sources.title: Red Flags of Investment Fraud Checklist
sources.evidence: Red flags: unlicensed professionals; aggressive sellers with false credentials; too good to be true; 'risk-free'; promises of great wealth and guaranteed returns; 'everyone is buying it'; pressure to invest right now; sensational pitches with fake testimonials; unsolicited pitches; asked to pay by credit card, gift card or wiring money abroad or to a personal account. Check professionals at Investor.gov.

sources.title: Beispiele für Anlagebetrug
sources.evidence: Offers to recover losses as a nasty trick: lists of defrauded investors circulate and are sold to new fraudsters; victims usually lose a second time (new money, fees). Misuse of FINMA's name: FINMA generally does not contact private individuals; uses @finma.ch emails; is never involved in offers to recover losses. Cloned websites: check imprint, contacts and URL. 'Im Zweifel Hände weg.'

sources.title: Woche 49: Einsatz von künstlicher Intelligenz für Betrugsversuche
sources.publisher: Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS, then NCSC)
sources.evidence: Images and videos can be made from photos of real people (e.g. from social media); videos from little base material; famous people misused in investment ads and give-away scams; voices cloned from voice samples, e.g. from phone calls; used in shock calls where a fake police officer plays a fabricated recording of the son or daughter.

sources.title: European Cyber Security Month: Tipps für Seniorinnen und Senioren
sources.evidence: Shock calls reach a new dimension with AI: software creates a same-sounding voice from one or more voice samples; criminals call with the voice of relatives and claim an emergency; voice samples from social media or other public sources; contact details mostly from the public phone book. Signs: metallic, monotone voice; strange content; untypical vocabulary. Tips: don't trust every caller; call the relative back on the known number; end implausible calls immediately; don't be intimidated or pressured; never give passwords or PIN on the phone; never give strangers access to your computer.

sources.title: Woche 31: Was die Zukunft bringt – Interaktion im KI-Zeitalter
sources.evidence: Cloning a voice currently needs an audio file of about 10 seconds; interactive and real-time; reports to BACS still few, isolated cases, likely to change; CEO fraud with cloned voice and in isolated cases a cloned boss in a video conference. Shock calls: many convinced they recognised their child's voice; possibly cloned from social media videos, or stress makes people believe it; BACS can't verify whether AI was used. Silent calls: BACS knows of no cases where a simple 'hello' was used to clone a voice; they test whether a person answers. Lip sync not yet perfect and can be a sign; deepfake videos often show unnatural behaviour; watch gestures, facial expressions and typical expressions. Recommendations: don't trust every caller; call back on the known number; end implausible calls; don't be pressured; never give passwords or PIN by phone; never give strangers access to your computer.

sources.title: How to change your privacy settings
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) By default any user can see your profile photo; to change who can see last seen and online, profile photo, about, status: Settings > Privacy, tap the setting, select Everyone, My contacts, My contacts except…, or Nobody. My Contacts: only contacts from your address book can see it.

sources.title: Die Dargebotene Hand – 143
sources.evidence: Checked 2026-10-26: 'Darüber reden hilft. Wir sind immer für Sie da. Persönlich, anonym und vertraulich.' Call 143, chat or mail. Support in English: call 0800 143 000 from 6–11 pm.

sources.title: Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
sources.evidence: Checked 2026-10-26: the IC3 is the central hub for reporting cyber-enabled crime, run by the FBI. Scammers impersonate the IC3: the IC3 does not work with any non-law-enforcement entity, such as law firms or crypto services, to recover lost funds, and will never directly contact you for information or money.

sources.title: What To Do if You Were Scammed
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) The FTC will never threaten you or say you must transfer money to protect it. Bank transfer: report to your bank immediately, ask to reverse; card: report to issuer using the number on the back; gift card: contact issuer, keep card and receipt; crypto: contact exchange or ATM operator, report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Gave account password: create a new strong password (change it wherever reused) and turn on two-factor authentication. Gave computer access: update security software, run a scan, change passwords, turn on 2FA. Report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov; Social Security number misused: IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan.

sources.title: AARP Fraud Watch Network Helpline
sources.evidence: Checked 2026-10-26: helpline 877-908-3360, Monday–Friday 8 a.m.–8 p.m. ET; 'If you've been affected by a scam, you are not alone'; guidance and support, not investigation or case recovery; free, confidential online support groups.

sources.title: Report Cybercrime online
sources.evidence: (WebFetch.) If you have fallen victim to cybercrime, links lead to the reporting website of your country; mechanisms vary; where there is no online option, go to your local police station. Lists all EU member states.

sources.title: Joint statement concerning 116 006, the single European victim support line
sources.evidence: Since 30 November 2009, 116 006 has been the dedicated helpline for victims of crime throughout Europe; thirteen Member States had implemented it (as of 2022); provides through trained professionals initial information and care, anonymously and confidentially, in social, legal and psychological matters.

sources.title: If you think your Apple Account has been compromised
sources.evidence: Signs: notifications of activity you don't recognise, 2FA codes you didn't request, password no longer works. Steps: change your Apple Account password (strong and unique), or reset it; at account.apple.com update security info and remove devices you don't recognise; check you control every email and phone number; if you can't reset, go to iforgot.apple.com for account recovery.

sources.title: Secure a hacked or compromised Google Account
sources.evidence: If you can't sign in, use the account recovery page. Review activity: Google Account > Security & sign-in > Recent security events > Review security events; 'No, it wasn't me'. Review devices: Your devices > Manage devices. Turn on 2-Step Verification. Contact your bank or local authorities if banking or ID info was saved.

sources.title: Change your Apple Account password
sources.evidence: On iPhone: open Settings, tap [your name], tap Sign-In & Security, tap Change Password, follow the instructions; option Remove Other Devices; may need to wait one hour (Stolen Device Protection).

sources.title: Change or reset your password (Android)
sources.evidence: Open the device's Settings app; tap Google > your name > Manage your Google Account (or myaccount.google.com); tap Security & sign-in; under 'How you sign in to Google' tap Password; enter the new password, tap Change Password. After changing, you are signed out everywhere except devices used to verify it's you.

sources.title: Red Flags of Elder Abuse
sources.publisher: US Department of Justice, Elder Justice Initiative
sources.evidence: Warning signs of financial exploitation: sudden changes in bank accounts or banking practices, including an unexplained withdrawal of large sums of money; unexplained disappearance of funds or valuable possessions; bills left unpaid despite adequate financial resources; unexplained sudden transfer of assets; unexplained credit card charges. Emotional signs: being upset or agitated, extremely withdrawn, change in sleeping or eating habits, depression or anxiety. 'If you are in immediate danger, call 911.'

sources.title: Protecting Older Investors From Financial Exploitation
sources.evidence: A trusted contact person on your account puts your firm in a better position to keep your account safe; a trusted contact cannot make trades or decisions about your account, and is not a power of attorney; recommended for all investors; once money has been disbursed, it is very difficult to get it back.
